title: Self-disarming controls: a blocking check whose own refusal record satisfies the condition it checks for (voice-lint's AC13, #56)
content:
Landed at #56 (merged b5f6f52, PR #87). Recorded as its own security-domain entry because the defect CLASS is reusable well beyond voice-lint: a blocking control that decides 'has the required condition been satisfied' by scanning a shared record stream can, if its own refusal is itself written into that same stream, satisfy its own condition on the very next check -- disarming itself the instant it first fires. This was a Phase 2 round-1 SecOps VETO, the most serious verdict this issue produced.

THE CONCRETE INSTANCE. voice-lint.mjs's Stop hook decides whether an assistant message needs voice.md's shape by scanning the transcript backwards for the last human turn. Round 1's candidate predicate defined 'human turn' by EXCLUSION (not a known machine-record shape) rather than by positive identification. voice-lint's OWN Stop-hook refusal is itself written into the transcript as a user-role record (the hook's stderr becomes a synthetic follow-up turn). Under exclusion-based classification, that refusal record was never explicitly excluded, so it qualified as a 'human turn' -- meaning the very act of the control firing moved the turn boundary forward and silenced the control for any IDENTICAL message resent immediately after. Verified live: under round 1's predicate, a transcript containing [status write] -> [voice-lint's own refusal] -> [resent identical bad message] exits 0 on the resend. The control caught the defect once and then let the exact same defect through unchanged.

THE FIX: POSITIVE IDENTIFICATION, NEVER EXCLUSION. A record only advances the turn boundary when it is POSITIVELY provable to be owner-authored (see architecture--voice-lint-turn-scoping.json's isHumanTurnRecord for the six-clause predicate, keyed on the vendor's own origin.kind === 'human' provenance label plus type/isSidechain/isMeta/message.role/timestamp guards). Under this predicate the refusal record fails the origin clause (it carries no origin field at all) AND the isMeta clause (isMeta true), so it does not advance the boundary and the self-disarm closes. AC13 pins this as a PAIR (transcript with the refusal record present vs. removed, both must exit 2 identically) specifically so the fix cannot be verified by a cell that passes because everything went quiet on both sides.

THE GENERALISABLE PATTERN, for any future blocking control read against this project's own audit/log/transcript stream (Stop hooks, SubagentStop hooks, or any check that scans a record stream the CHECK ITSELF, or a sibling check, also writes into): (1) enumerate what the control's own refusal, or any other control's refusal, looks like as a RECORD in the stream it scans -- it is very often shaped just enough like the thing being verified that an exclusion-based classifier admits it by accident. (2) Never define the target condition by subtracting known noise from the record population; define it by asserting the POSITIVE, minimal set of properties that only the real target condition can have. Exclusion-based logic silently WIDENS to admit every future record shape nobody thought to exclude (including the control's own output); positive-identification logic silently NARROWS, which is the safe failure direction for a control whose worst failure mode is going quiet. (3) Write the self-disarm test as a PAIR (defect record present vs. absent, same expected verdict on both) rather than a single cell, because a single cell asserting 'still refuses with the defect record present' can pass by coincidence if the fix also broke something else that happens to keep the check loud.

SecOps's non-veto reasoning at Phase 4 for this same fix is also worth recording as a boundary case: SecOps explicitly did NOT veto the shipped fix's remaining declared residuals (R7 iv, the origin.kind trust residual; R7 iii-b, the mtime-preserving-restore residual) because this is a LOCAL dev-tool with no auth/data/privilege/compliance dimension, and it grants no new adversary capability -- the same local access that could exploit either residual already permits a cheaper disarm route (editing status.json directly). That is a categorically different judgment from the round-1 self-disarm veto, which was a functional-correctness defect in the control's own logic, not a residual risk under an access model. Do not conflate 'declared residual, non-blocking' with 'self-disarm, blocking' when triaging a similar finding in a future control -- the self-disarm class blocks because it makes the control worse than absent (it creates false confidence that a check ran and passed), while a declared residual with a stated expiry is an honest, bounded gap.
